title: Isidore the Farmer (15 May)
hookLine: a Spanish farmworker whose ploughing, legend says, angels helped with while he prayed

lines: A SECOND PLOW IN THE FIELD.
cards: What does a landowner do when his workers complain about one of their own? This one, near Madrid, rides out early in the morning to check on his hired man. The hired man, they say, comes late to the fields every day.
He stops at church first. So the landowner goes to see for himself. And here the story turns into legend.
Out in the field, the hired man's plow is moving. Beside it, another plow, pulled by white oxen, driven by figures nobody can name.

teach.b: Isidore worked land that belonged to someone else. Tradition says he married a woman named Maria, who is honored too, and that the two of them lived simply and shared what little they had.
That's close to all the story needs. He left no writings and held no office. He plowed.

teach.h: A LEGEND POINTING AT SOMETHING TRUE.
teach.b: The legend of the angels comes in more than one version, and it isn't in scripture. It's a story people have loved, told to point at something. Not that prayer gets you out of work: Isidore still plows.
It points at the old worry he had to face, that time given to God is time stolen from the job. In the legend the field doesn't suffer. The work gets done.

teach.h: UNLESS THE LORD BUILD THE HOUSE.
teach.b: A line in the Psalms, in the Douay-Rheims, fits a farm as well as a building site: "Unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it." The farmer's version would be: unless the Lord plows the field.

Isidore's story takes that literally, with oxen. Other stories told about him lean the same way. Tradition says he poured out grain for hungry birds in winter, and his sack was still full when he reached the mill.

teach.h: PATRON OF THOSE WHO GROW OUR FOOD.
teach.b: Catholics have made him a patron of farmers and of the people who grow what everyone else eats, often without anyone noticing.
It's a story about a hired hand who believed the God he prayed to was also out in the field.

how: Catholics in farming areas often keep Saint Isidore's day on 15 May with Masses and blessings of fields, animals or tractors, and pray for farmers and a good harvest.

o: a hired farmhand near Madrid who prayed before plowing
a Spanish landowner who gave his fields to the poor
a bishop of Seville who wrote a great encyclopedia

games.q: Isidore the Farmer — tap the pairs.
p: rides out to check on him

s: the landowner rode out because Isidore asked him to
the other workers complained that he came late, so the landowner went to see for himself.
in the legend, Isidore's field suffers because he prays
the work gets done. that's the point of the story.
Isidore was a farmworker on someone else's land
he was a hired hand who plowed another man's land.

games.q: you're the landowner. your workers say your hired man stops at church every morning and comes late. what do you do?
o: ride out and see for yourself.
games.why: he rides out to check, and the legend says he finds a second plow at work beside Isidore's.

practice: Think back to your last meal, choose one thing on the plate, and follow it backward: a truck, a packing shed, a field, someone bending in the heat or up before dawn, worried about rain.
You'll never know their name; hold them anyway. If you pray, ask Saint Isidore to pray for farmers and farmworkers; if you don't, simply let them be seen by you.

wordCard.voice: Isidore, the farmer of Madrid. A hired hand who prayed before he plowed, and whose field, legend says, angels helped to plow.

carryVoice: Your line: angels plow. In his story, prayer and work share one field. That's day nine hundred ninety.
